social_history.living_situation: Single, lives alone; sister staying with her now

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Anxious but cooperative.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Mild bilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness — forehead involved bilaterally. Voice slightly nasal. Gag reflex diminished bilaterally. No diplopia, no ptosis.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral proximal lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3+/5, hip abduction 4/5. Knee extension 4/5. Ankle dorsiflexion 4-/5. Bilateral upper extremity: shoulder abduction 4/5, grip 4+/5.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral glove-and-stocking paresthesias and reduced pinprick sensation. Vibration reduced at bilateral malleoli.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral Achilles reflexes. Absent bilateral patellar reflexes. Trace bilateral brachioradialis. Absent bilateral biceps. All deep tendon reflexes markedly diminished or absent — global areflexia.
neurological_exam.gait: Requires bilateral arm support to walk 10 feet. Unable to rise from chair without armrest.
neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 2.0 L (predicted 3.2 L — 63% of predicted). NIF: -32 cmH2O. Currently just above intubation threshold but declining over past 24 hours.

patient.chief_complaint: Eight-day progressive ascending weakness and sensory loss with bilateral facial weakness and areflexia, preceded by gastroenteritis.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. J. is a 42-year-old nurse presenting with an 8-day history of progressive ascending neurological symptoms. Three weeks ago she had a gastrointestinal illness with diarrhea lasting 4 days, which resolved. One week later, she noticed bilateral foot tingling. As a nurse, she was appropriately alarmed and came to the ED when she noticed difficulty rising from the toilet two days ago. Over the past 8 days, weakness has ascended from her feet to her thighs. She noted bilateral facial weakness when brushing her teeth this morning — both sides of her face are affected. She has difficulty swallowing thin liquids and has been coughing with water. She denies shortness of breath at rest but feels slightly breathless with exertion. She has no sphincter symptoms. She denies any tick exposure. Her prior flu vaccination was 3 months ago. She knows about GBS from nursing training and suspects the diagnosis. Symptoms have been relentlessly progressive.

specialized_test.impression: Severe demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy meeting diagnostic criteria for AIDP. Absent F-waves and H-reflex indicate proximal involvement. Bilateral absent sural SNAPs. This is moderate-to-severe AIDP requiring immediate treatment.

findings: QTc prolonged at 462 ms — significant in context of GBS autonomic dysfunction
ecg.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia with prolonged QTc in setting of GBS. Continuous telemetry required. QTc lengthening warrants avoidance of QT-prolonging medications.

quantitative_data.CMAP_change: -50% amplitude from baseline — secondary axonal injury

output.impression: Repeat NCS shows further deterioration with CMAP amplitude reduction suggestive of secondary axonal injury superimposed on AIDP. This is consistent with anti-GM1/GD1a-associated GBS. Prognosis more guarded — recovery may be slower.

output.rhythm_summary: Sinus tachycardia alternating with bradycardia episodes. Labile blood pressure 80-180 mmHg systolic.

events.event: Sinus bradycardia 38 bpm — 4 minutes, associated with suctioning
Hypertensive crisis: BP 196/110 mmHg — treated with IV labetalol
Hypotension: BP 80/50 mmHg — IV fluids given

findings: Bradycardia triggered by vagal stimuli (suctioning, turning)
output.impression: Severe autonomic instability — ICU-level care mandatory. Avoid vagal stimulation. Treat BP extremes cautiously. Pacing equipment on standby.
recommended_actions: Cautious antihypertensive use — short-acting agents preferred

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP with secondary axonal injury (post-Campylobacter jejuni), requiring mechanical ventilation

differential.key_features: 8-day acute onset — too rapid for CIDP
No sensory level, no UMN signs, areflexia rather than hyperreflexia
Sensory symptoms present; NCS shows demyelinating pattern
TSH normal; pattern is neuropathic not myopathic; areflexia

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Campylobacter positive; hyponatremia, hypokalemia to correct

optimal_actions.action: ICU admission and intubation when NIF crosses threshold

critical_actions: ICU admission required — this patient will need intubation (NIF crossing threshold)
Correct hyponatremia and hypokalemia — cardiac arrhythmia risk in autonomic GBS
Do NOT delay IVIG waiting for CSF results
Intubate electively rather than emergently — patients who reach respiratory failure should be intubated before crisis
Avoid QT-prolonging medications — QTc already 462 ms
contraindicated_actions: Sedating medications before intubation — respiratory compromise risk
key_reasoning_points: Bilateral facial diplegia, ascending areflexia, and sensory symptoms after Campylobacter gastroenteritis is classic GBS presentation
The moderate case challenge: hyponatremia may suggest SIADH (GBS association) rather than dilutional — requires careful management
NIF crossing -25 cmH2O threshold = elective intubation; do not wait for CO2 retention
High-titer anti-GM1/GD1a predicts secondary axonal injury and prolonged recovery — counsel patient accordingly
Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's) is a red herring — TSH is normal and the weakness is neuropathic not myopathic
